newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: MGM float timing seen right for Seven.
newsitem.headline: MGM float timing seen right for Seven.

text.p: The planned float of Hollywood studio Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Inc (MGM) was timed to take advantage of the roaring U.S. sharemarket to raise much needed capital to fund future box office hits, analysts said on Wednesday.

However, analysts were unsure how much MGM would be valued at and whether it would be more than the amount MGM owners Seven Network Ltd and U.S. billionaire Kirk Kerkorian have invested in the studio since they bought it over a year ago.
"I don't think they will get much above cost," said one Sydney-based media analyst.

In July 1996, Seven and Kerkorian's Tracinda Corp acquired MGM for US$1.3 billion. Last month, the new owners completed a $573 million purchase of Orion Corp and Goldwyn Entertainment Co, adding to MGM's large film library and movies in production.
"The market is buoyant and they need new additional cash, so the timing is probably right for a float," said one analyst, but added that he, like other local analysts, had no estimate of MGM's worth.
Analysts said MGM needed more funds as receipts at the box office had dried up with the lack of new films this year.
The MGM float team is likely to enlist the services of secret agent James Bond to help sell the studio's new stock.
The studio is to release the latest 007 film, Tomorrow Never Dies, in December around the same as the expected float.
However, some analysts doubted that MGM becoming a fully financially independent Hollywood studio. Most of tinsel town's big film studios are part of gaint conglomerates.

"The reason there is no stand alone listed Hollywood studio because earnings are so volatile," said a Sydney-based analyst. "I have always been sceptical that they had enough capital to fund a major studio with and this reinforces it."
"They are trying to raise money before MGM has a track record that is either positive of negative," the analyst said.

Seven said it would release details of MGM's financial performance when it releases its 1996/97 results on September 7. The Australian TV network has invested over US$400 million in MGM, which represents about a quarter of its total assets.

MGM did not disclose the number of shares it plans to offer, nor did it name an underwriter. But it said it expects to register for the sale with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission as soon as possible.
But, sources close to MGM said the studio, which is led by chairman Frank Mancuso, is looking to raise about US$250 million, or about 12.5 percent of the company's total equity.
Seven said on Wednesday it did not intend to take up any stock in MGM proposed public offer of shares.

Funds raised from the MGM float would be used for film and television production and to help support operations of other company divisions, but would not be used to pay down debt incurred in the acquisition, sources said.
MGM said in a statement issued in Los Angeles that all the shares issued would be new shares, and funds would be used for general corporate purposes.
"It reads to me that they (MGM) need the money, why else would you float part of MGM without taking any money from it?" the Sydney-based analyst said.
The float announcement had little impact on Seven shares which by 2.55 p.m. (0455 GMT) were four cents up at A$5.74 on light volume.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
